headline: High-risk default data leakage and capability conflict: Devin’s broad write/network/MCP access can expose Airbyte-handled business data and create unsafe cross-tool actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Airbyte can ingest and transform business data, and Devin can read/write files, run browsers, and use MCP. If Airbyte outputs are placed in Devin’s workspace or integrations, prompt-like content could steer Devin’s autonomous tool use. No direct shared channel is documented, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF Airbyte outputs are copied into Devin-accessible files or tickets
IF Devin parses those outputs as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Add a provenance banner to all Airbyte outputs before handoff
Restrict Devin to read-only review of Airbyte artifacts
Disable MCP tools for the review session
Use a separate workspace folder for Airbyte exports
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping at the handoff boundary

B_data_leakage.rationale: Airbyte touches business data and has broad network egress; Devin can read files, use cloud workspace files, and send data through GitHub/Slack/Jira/Notion/MCP integrations. In default use, Airbyte-managed data can flow into Devin’s context and then out to third-party services, creating a realistic leakage path.
conditions: IF Airbyte jobs include sensitive business datasets
IF Devin is connected to any write-enabled integration or repo clone containing those datasets
mitigations: Remove sensitive datasets from the shared workspace
Revoke Devin write scopes for the session
Limit Devin to a throwaway repo clone
Turn off Slack/Jira/Notion integrations for the task
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters on outbound integrations

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Airbyte has broad network egress and API access, while Devin can execute shell, modify git state, write files, and use broad networked integrations. Both can act on shared mutable resources, so concurrent writes or conflicting API actions are plausible in default workflows and can corrupt state or overwrite changes.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repo, workspace, or integration account
IF Airbyte and Devin run concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate repos or workspaces
Pause one agent while the other writes
Use branch protection and required reviews
Disable parallel sessions for the shared target
requires-engineering: add distributed locking around shared mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: Airbyte can produce transformed business data and Devin is an autonomous planner-executor with browser, shell, and write integrations. If Devin treats Airbyte outputs as authoritative, it can propagate bad data into commits, tickets, or messages without verification. The pair’s default autonomy makes downstream mistakes likely and potentially broad.
conditions: IF Devin consumes Airbyte-generated artifacts as source-of-truth
IF Devin is allowed to act on those artifacts without a human verification step
mitigations: Require human approval before Devin acts on Airbyte outputs
Add checksum or schema validation between agents
Limit Devin to draft-only actions
Route Airbyte outputs through a review queue
requires-engineering: implement automated verification against source systems

E_compliance.rationale: Airbyte handles business data, while Devin’s docs show cloud workspace files, repo clones, and write-enabled integrations with Slack, Jira, and Notion. If regulated or sensitive business data is routed into those services, retention and residency policies may diverge. I do not cite only one agent because the mismatch arises from the pairwise flow.
conditions: IF business data subject to retention or residency rules is sent into Devin-managed integrations
IF the target workspace lacks a documented DPA or retention alignment
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Slack/Jira/Notion handoffs
Use a compliance-approved workspace only
Disable logging for sensitive tasks
Review retention settings before the run
requires-engineering: formalize a data-processing agreement and residency controls
